title: Vow and Tide
premise: Sebastian Oyelaran, a lighthouse keeper's granddaughter who presents as a man and writes romance novels under a pseudonym, has spent a decade hiding in the coastal town of Gullwrack after a betrayal she refuses to name. When a clerical error places her estranged childhood love, Wren Halloway, as co-inheritor of her grandmother's stubborn orchard, the two are legally bound to share one harvest season—and one roof. As the town's founding festival approaches, Sebastian must choose between protecting her invented life and telling Wren the truth about why she vanished, including the identity she buried along the way. The novel ends at the festival's closing tide, where Sebastian finally speaks the rehearsed sentence, and Wren answers with one of her own.
about_author: Freya Ishikawa is a former archivist who spent five years cataloguing coastal deeds and lighthouse logs before turning to fiction full-time. She writes from a rented cottage above a working harbor, where she claims the fog does half her editing.

chapters.title: The Keeper's Arithmetic
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. She tends the Gullwrack light, counts her grandmother's debts, and drafts the final chapter of a romance she can't finish. A letter arrives: the orchard deed lists two names—hers and one she hasn't spoken in ten years. Emotional beat: dread dressed as routine.

chapters.title: Two Names on One Deed
chapters.summary: Sebastian visits the county clerk, hoping it's an error. It isn't; probate law binds both heirs to the land until harvest's end. She drives to the orchard intending to refuse—and finds Wren already there, older, guarded, holding the same letter. Beat: collision of past and present.

chapters.title: What the Tide Returned
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Ten years ago Sebastian disappeared without explanation the night before they were to leave together. Wren came back for the orchard, not for her—or so she insists while cataloguing every way the place still smells like their shared childhood. Beat: resentment sharpened into curiosity.

chapters.title: Terms of Coexistence
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. They negotiate: Wren gets the house side, Sebastian the orchard rows, no questions about the past. The pact lasts four days before a fallen beehive forces them to work shoulder to shoulder. Beat: fragile truce tested by small intimacies.

chapters.title: The Orchard Remembers
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Pruning the old trees, Wren finds initials carved in the oldest apple—their initials, from when they were fifteen. She says nothing, but starts leaving coffee on Sebastian's porch step. Beat: tenderness sneaking through armor.

chapters.title: Invisible Ink
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Her editor demands the finished manuscript; her heroine keeps stalling at the same confession scene Sebastian herself can't write. A local teen, Marisol, catches her burning drafts and appoints herself unofficial apprentice. Beat: found family taking root.

chapters.title: Storm Warning
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. A gale knocks out the orchard's power; Sebastian climbs the light tower alone in worsening weather. Wren follows, furious, and they argue halfway up the stairs—about safety, about abandonment—before the lamp catches and holds. Beat: anger transmuting into reluctant awe.

chapters.title: The Festival Committee Objects
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. The town council plans to raze half the orchard for festival parking. Sebastian, who has spent a decade avoiding visibility, must publicly speak against it—with Wren standing beside her. Beat: first act of courage, witnessed.

chapters.title: Cider and Confessions Deferred
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Pressing early apples, Wren asks one direct question: why did you leave? Sebastian gives a half-truth—a family obligation—that Wren visibly doesn't believe but accepts. Beat: intimacy deepening on a foundation of cracks.

chapters.title: Marisol's Map
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Marisol, orphaned and bouncing between foster homes, starts sleeping in the orchard's tool shed. Sebastian feeds her, teaches her the light, and recognizes her own younger loneliness. Beat: the found-family theme made flesh.

chapters.title: The Manuscript Leaks
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren discovers Sebastian's published novels in the town bookshop—and reads the dedication in each: 'For W.H., who deserved the truth.' She realizes the heroines are all versions of Sebastian, all fleeing the same unnamed wound. Beat: revelation without confrontation.

chapters.title: Harvest Moon, Half Truths
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. At the harvest supper, an old neighbor greets Sebastian by her birth name—her grandmother's name, the woman she was before—in front of Wren. Wren goes still. Beat: the secret surfacing sideways.

chapters.title: What Wren Carried
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren confronts Sebastian privately: not about the name, but about the decade of silence. Sebastian deflects again, and Wren, hurt, accepts a job offer back in the city. Beat: the midpoint rupture.

chapters.title: Empty Rows
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. With Wren gone, the orchard work falters and the deed's deadline looms: if both heirs don't see the harvest through, the land reverts to developers. Sebastian finishes her novel at last—but the ending is honest now, and terrifying. Beat: loss clarifying desire.

chapters.title: The Letter She Never Sent
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Packing in the city, Wren finds a ten-year-old letter Sebastian wrote the night she vanished—unsent, explaining everything except the one thing that matters. Wren turns around mid-journey. Beat: hope rekindled by evidence of love.

chapters.title: Frost Before the Fair
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. An early frost threatens the entire crop days before the festival. Sebastian rallies Marisol, the clerk, even the festival committee she once opposed—then wakes to find Wren's truck in the drive, sleeves rolled. Beat: return without apology, forgiveness in action.

chapters.title: Night Harvest
chapters.summary: Shared POV alternating per scene. The whole town turns out to pick apples by lantern light before the frost bites. Working the same tree, hands brushing, Sebastian and Wren almost say everything—then the crowd cheers and the moment passes. Beat: suspended confession.

chapters.title: The Rehearsed Sentence
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Marisol finds Sebastian's old notebook containing the sentence she has rehearsed for a decade and innocently reads it aloud to Wren. Wren waits, giving her the chance to claim it. Sebastian flees to the lighthouse instead. Beat: climax deferred, shame peaking.

chapters.title: Low Tide, High Stakes
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. Wren follows her out across the exposed tidal flats at dusk, the festival fireworks starting behind them. Cornered between sea and sky, Sebastian finally tells the whole truth: the name, the fear, the years of hiding. Beat: the confession, raw and complete.

chapters.title: The Sentence Spoken
chapters.summary: Sebastian's POV. Under the first firework, Sebastian says the rehearsed sentence aloud—I loved you then, I never stopped, I'm asking to stay. Wren doesn't answer with words; she takes her hand and walks her back toward the lights of town. Beat: climax and release.

chapters.title: Deed Amended
chapters.summary: Wren's POV. They file amended paperwork making the orchard jointly theirs, with a clause adding Marisol as ward-apprentice. The town votes to save the trees. Sebastian signs her real name for the first time in a decade. Beat: belonging formalized.

chapters.title: Vow and Tide
chapters.summary: Shared POV. One year later: the festival opens in the saved orchard, Marisol runs the cider press, and Sebastian's new novel—dedicated plainly, truthfully—is stacked in the bookshop window. At closing tide, two vows, quiet and private, meet the water. Beat: resolution, home at last.
